paraphrase: The Māheśvaras are four - Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Kāruṇika-siddhāntins and Kāpālikas - all following doctrines taught by Maheśvara. For them the cause is the Lord; the effect is mahat and the rest derived from primal matter; yoga is meditation and fixation on Oṃ and the like; the rule runs from bathing thrice daily to the hidden conduct; the end of suffering is release, the loosing of the paśus' bond. Their reasoning: a conscious agent like a potter is only the efficient cause of a pot, so the Lord is only the efficient cause of the world.

original.text: māheśvarāś catvāraḥ - śaivāḥ pāśupatāḥ kāruṇikasiddhāntinaḥ kāpālikāś ceti

paraphrase: The jīva is Brahman delimited (avacchinna) by the inner organ, as space is delimited by a pot; Brahman itself is untouched by the delimitation.
Ignorance resides in the individual selves with Brahman as its object; the jīva and ignorance presuppose each other beginninglessly, like seed and sprout; there are as many ignorances as jīvas.
notes: Topic-level reference (commentary on the adhyāsa-bhāṣya and passim).

paraphrase: The knowledge produced by the Upaniṣadic sentence is mediate; the mind, perfected by sustained contemplation and aided by hearing and reflection, is the instrument of direct realization, as scripture says 'it is to be seen by the mind alone'.

paraphrase: Salutation to Brahman — immeasurable bliss and knowledge, deathless — which, accompanied by two indescribable ignorances, is the source whose apparent transformations are space, air, fire, water and earth, and from which this whole moving and unmoving world has come.
Sacrifice, gifts and austerity (BĀU 4.4.22) produce the desire to know (vividiṣā) by purifying the mind; they do not produce knowledge itself.
notes: Topic-level reference; the Vivaraṇa holds that they lead to knowledge (vedana) itself.
